tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

## Tested Models

![Small models run at full precision or Q8, medium at Q4_K_M, large at Q4_0 or multi-GPU](docs/images/readme/model-sizing.png)

A K80 has **12 GB VRAM per GPU** (24 GB for a dual-GPU board). Size quantization to fit:

| Model size    | Quantization         |
|---------------|----------------------|
| Small (1–4B)  | Full precision or Q8 |
| Medium (7–8B) | Q4_K_M               |
| Large (13B+)  | Q4_0 or multi-GPU    |

Verified on K80: `gemma3:4b`, `gemma3:27b`, `gemma4:e4b`, `gemma4:26b`, `qwen3.5:9b`,
`qwen3.5:27b`, `qwen3.8:27b`, `gpt-oss:20b`, `deepseek-r1:7b`, `ministral-3`, `functiongemma`.

## How It's Built

Ollama37 is split into two Docker images so the thing you run stays small:

![Source compiles in a ~15 GB builder image into a ~1 GB runtime image, published to Docker Hub](docs/images/readme/build-pipeline.png)

- **`ollama37-builder` (~15 GB)** — the build environment only: CUDA 11.4 toolkit, GCC 10
  and CMake 4 (compiled from source, ~90 min the first time), and Go. It is never shipped.
- **`ollama37` (~1 GB)** — a multi-stage build. The code is compiled *inside* the builder
  with the `CUDA 11 K80` preset (native CUBIN for `sm_37`–`sm_86`, the 470 datacenter sweep), then only the
  artifacts — the `ollama` binary, the GGML/CUDA libraries, the bundled CUDA runtime libs
  (cuBLAS, cuBLASLt, cudart), and the GCC 10 runtime libs — are copied onto a slim
  `rockylinux:8-minimal` base. This is the image published to Docker Hub.

To build it yourself:

```bash
cd docker
make build          # builds the builder image (first time only), then the runtime image
docker compose up -d
```

## Building for other GPUs

The published image now targets the whole 470-era datacenter range (`sm_37` through
`sm_86`, Kepler through Ampere), but **only the K80 is tested** — the other architectures
are compiled in and should load, yet are unvalidated, so you are on your own there.

For cards **outside** that range — Ada (RTX 40-series) and Hopper (H100), which need
CUDA 12+ and a newer driver — you have to build it yourself: `CMakePresets.json` ships
`CUDA 12` / `CUDA 13` presets for them. Note that moving to a newer CUDA/driver **drops
K80 support** — the very thing this project pins CUDA 11.4 / driver 470 to keep. See
[docker/README.md](docker/README.md).

## Troubleshooting

The most common K80 snag: `nvidia-smi` works inside the container but Ollama reports **0
GPUs**, because the host is missing the UVM device files. Fix it on the host with:

```bash
nvidia-modprobe -u -c=0
```

This and other issues (GPU not detected, model load failures, build problems) are covered
in [docker/README.md](docker/README.md#troubleshooting).

Issues and pull requests are welcome — Tesla K80 compatibility reports and fixes
especially. See the [issue tracker](https://github.com/dogkeeper886/ollama37/issues).

content.content:
---
paths:
  - ".github/workflows/**/*.yml"
  - ".github/actions/**/*.yml"
---

# CI Workflow Patterns

ollama37's CI is organized by **test suite**, with a pipeline workflow that chains the suites,
plus separate perf/experiment workflows. All run on a labelled self-hosted GPU runner — see
[Host selection](#host-selection).

## Suite workflows + the pipeline

```
.github/workflows/
├── test-build.yml        # build suite     (toolchain image, runtime image, image sizes)
├── test-runtime.yml      # runtime suite   (container, GPU detection, health, /api/metrics)
├── test-inference.yml    # inference suite (model pull + GPU inference smoke)
├── test-models.yml       # models suite    (per-model regression on K80)
└── test-pipeline.yml     # full pipeline: build → runtime → inference → models (via needs:)
```

Each suite workflow runs the TypeScript runner (`cli.ts run`) filtered by `--suite`. The
pipeline chains the suites with job `needs:` dependencies; the inference/models suites are the
ones that exercise the agent judge.

**Adding a suite test:** add a `TC-<SUITE>-NNN.yml` under `cicd/tests/testcases/<suite>/` (via
`ci-testcase`) — no workflow change needed; the suite workflow picks it up by `--suite`.

## Perf / experiment workflows

Performance and capability experiments run via the runner's perf subcommands, separate from the
suite workflows:

```
├── test-throughput.yml   # cli.ts bench-throughput — per-model tok/s + output check (short prompt)
├── test-context.yml      # cli.ts bench-context — long-context prefill/decode tok/s + needle + judge
├── test-mcp.yml          # cli.ts test-mcp — MCP tool-call capability (one model list x one ctx/batch)
└── test-report-sweep.yml # loops model x context (x num_batch, opt-in) — fills the k80-*-by-family tables + the num_batch x context fit map
```

`test-context.yml` is the flash-attention path comparison: it primes a realistic long prompt (so
prefill and decode are in the regime where FA's cost/benefit shows) and is self-contained — it
applies the experiment env (`flash_attention`/`kv_cache_type`) by recreating the container, then
`always()` reverts to the stable baseline (FA off). `test-throughput.yml` stays the short-prompt K80
model-regression tool.

`test-report-sweep.yml` is a MEASUREMENT sweep, not a gate — kept out of the pipeline because MCP
T2 legitimately fails for weaker models. It loops every model x context serially, and (opt-in via
`fit_map_models`) adds a **fit-map** pass: per model it bounds the context ladder to the trained
window and gates on tool support — skipping no-tools models (`cli.ts model-bounds`, via
`/api/show`) — then loops `num_batch` x bounded-context, one `test-mcp` cell each with the
structural judge. `aggregate-sweep.py` derives each cell's
fit (✅ on GPU / ⚠️ CPU spill / ❌ OOM) from the MCP GPU snapshot (per-die VRAM + offload%, captured
independent of the correctness verdict), emitting the fit-map table for a human to commit. The
default sweep (no `fit_map_models`) is unchanged.

`release-docker.yml` builds and publishes the image on a release.

## Host selection

There is more than one possible GPU testbed, so **never use a bare `runs-on: self-hosted`.**
It matches any runner, and a K80 sweep landing on a small consumer card produces numbers that
look valid and are not.

Select the host by the compute capability it provides:

```yaml
runs-on: [self-hosted, sm37]      # Tesla K80 — the only hardware-validated target
```

| Label | Host | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `sm37` | Tesla K80 box (`rocky8-k80-cicd-1`) | 4 dies, ~11.4 GiB each. The reference testbed. |
| `sm61` | host B, GTX 1080 Ti (`rocky9-1080ti-cicd-1`) | 1 card, 11 GiB. `models` suite only. |
| `sm86` | host B, RTX 3060 (`rocky9-3060-cicd-1`) | 1 card, 12 GiB. `models` suite only. |

A workflow that can run on more than one testbed takes a `runner_label` input defaulting to
`sm37`, and uses `runs-on: [self-hosted, "${{ inputs.runner_label || 'sm37' }}"]`.

**Not every suite fits every host.** Host B's cards also serve the agent judge's `ollama`, so
`sm61` and `sm86` run only `test-models.yml`: its Yield GPU / Restore GPU steps lend one card to
the test, and the runner's `OLLAMA37_TEST_IDS` limits the suite to the models that fit. Workflows
that `docker compose up` (runtime, build, perf) are not set up there, and host B runs one job at a
time (both cards share port 11434). The `build` suite is a multi-hour no-cache compile that belongs
on `sm37` where the builder image is cached.

**Order of operations when adding a runner:** add the label to the runner *first*, then pin
workflows to it. Pinning to a label no runner carries makes every job queue forever.

# CI Workflow Patterns

plus separate perf/experiment workflows. All run on a labelled self-hosted GPU runner — see
[Host selection](#host-selection).

## Suite workflows + the pipeline

```
.github/workflows/
├── test-build.yml        # build suite     (toolchain image, runtime image, image sizes)
├── test-runtime.yml      # runtime suite   (container, GPU detection, health, /api/metrics)
├── test-inference.yml    # inference suite (model pull + GPU inference smoke)
├── test-models.yml       # models suite    (per-model regression on K80)
└── test-pipeline.yml     # full pipeline: build → runtime → inference → models (via needs:)
```

Each suite workflow runs the TypeScript runner (`cli.ts run`) filtered by `--suite`. The
pipeline chains the suites with job `needs:` dependencies; the inference/models suites are the
ones that exercise the agent judge.

**Adding a suite test:** add a `TC-<SUITE>-NNN.yml` under `cicd/tests/testcases/<suite>/` (via
`ci-testcase`) — no workflow change needed; the suite workflow picks it up by `--suite`.

## Perf / experiment workflows

Performance and capability experiments run via the runner's perf subcommands, separate from the
suite workflows:

```
├── test-throughput.yml   # cli.ts bench-throughput — per-model tok/s + output check (short prompt)
├── test-context.yml      # cli.ts bench-context — long-context prefill/decode tok/s + needle + judge
├── test-mcp.yml          # cli.ts test-mcp — MCP tool-call capability (one model list x one ctx/batch)
└── test-report-sweep.yml # loops model x context (x num_batch, opt-in) — fills the k80-*-by-family tables + the num_batch x context fit map
```

`test-context.yml` is the flash-attention path comparison: it primes a realistic long prompt (so
prefill and decode are in the regime where FA's cost/benefit shows) and is self-contained — it

`always()` reverts to the stable baseline (FA off). `test-throughput.yml` stays the short-prompt K80
model-regression tool.

# Porting upstream code to the K80

This fork runs Ollama on the **Tesla K80** — compute capability **sm_37**, CUDA 11.4,
GCC 10, **no tensor cores**, 12 GB per die. Porting upstream code onto that hardware has
two disciplines. The first is about *getting it to build*; the second — the one most
easily skipped — is about *confirming it's actually faster*.

## 1. Port the source; don't adapt the environment

Vendor the upstream files into our tree and rewrite each one to compile with the
**existing** toolchain (nvcc 11.4 / GCC 10 / C++17 / sm_37, with cuBLAS or SIMT
fallbacks where tensor cores would be used). Mirror how `ml/backend/ggml` already vendors
and patches ggml in-tree.

Do **not** change the builder image, pull upstream source unmodified, or otherwise bend
the environment to the code. The fork exists to make code run on constrained hardware — if
using upstream unmodified were acceptable, upstream Ollama would already be the answer.

## 2. Benchmark every ported optimization on the K80 — it may be a net *loss*

Upstream optimizations are tuned for modern GPUs (tensor cores, large register files,
kernels written for Ampere/Hopper). On sm_37 an "optimization" can be **slower** than the
naive path it replaces. Building and producing correct output is **not** evidence that a
ported optimization helps — measure it.

**Worked example — flash attention.** Both upstream and our own `docker/.env.example`
assumed FA was a small win ("~3% tok/s"). On the K80 it is the opposite: for `gemma4:26b`,
FA is a ~22% loss at short context and a **7.4× loss** at a 6,800-token prompt (1.18 vs
8.74 tok/s decode; a 25-minute tool-calling run drops to under 3 minutes with FA off). The
"optimization" was the bottleneck. See **#337**.

**Rule:** when you port or enable an optimization — a flash-attention path, a fused kernel,
a tensor-core routine, a KV-cache quantization — benchmark it on the K80 against the path
it replaces, and keep it only if it actually wins. Don't trust upstream's performance
assumptions or in-code comments; they were written for different silicon.

## 3. Measure at realistic context lengths, not just short prompts

The FA regression was only +22% at a short prompt but **7.4×** at 6,800 tokens — a
short-prompt benchmark would have hidden it. Attention-related costs scale with context, so

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

content.content:
# Ollama37 Build Configuration
# Copy this file to .env and customize as needed
#
# Usage:
#   cp .env.example .env
#   # Edit .env with your values
#   make build

# Ollama version to embed in the binary
# This version is displayed by 'ollama --version' and in logs
OLLAMA_VERSION=2.2.1

# --- Runtime tuning (optional; container reads these via docker compose) ---
# Defaults are tuned for K80 hardware. Override here only if you know what
# you're doing.

# Flash attention. Left unset by default — ollama's hardware gate forces it OFF on
# the K80 (sm_37) regardless (a net loss there, ~7x slower at long context; see #346).
# On cc>=7.0 cards (the widened build, experimental) set =1 to enable FA.
# OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1

# KV cache element type. Default "f16" on K80, because FA is off there and
# V-cache quantization (q8_0) requires FA — so q8_0 won't load on the K80.
# f16 costs ~2x the KV memory of q8_0; if a large model + long context doesn't
# fit on a 12GB die, reduce num_ctx. q8_0/q4_0 are only usable on FA-capable
# (cc>=7.0) cards.
# OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=f16

# Verbose server logging.
# OLLAMA_DEBUG=1
=== compose ===
services:
  ollama:
    image: dogkeeper886/ollama37:latest
    # any container name; default ollama37
    container_name: ${OLLAMA37_CONTAINER:-ollama37}
    runtime: nvidia
    deploy:
      resources:
        reservations:
          devices:
            - driver: nvidia
              count: all
              capabilities: [gpu]
    ports:
      - "11434:11434"
    volumes:
      - ollama-data:/root/.ollama
    environment:
      - OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434
      - OLLAMA_DEBUG=${OLLAMA_DEBUG:-}
      # K80 perf defaults — see docker/.env.example to override.
      # Flash attention is left unset (not pinned): ollama's hardware gate forces it
      # off on the K80 (sm_37) anyway — it's a net loss there (see #346) — and we don't
      # auto-enable it on the experimental cc>=7.0 cards. Set OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1
      # to turn it on where supported. With FA off, q8_0 KV needs FA, so cache is f16.
      - OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=${OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION:-}
      - OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=${OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE:-f16}
      # Compute-buffer safety margin (#352). The built-in default 2.5 keeps large
      # models (deepseek-r1:32b) on the K80's small dies instead of offloading to CPU.
      # Raising it over-reserves and re-triggers that offload; lowering it too far
      # risks "failed to allocate compute buffers". Unset = use the built-in 2.5 default.
      - OLLAMA_GRAPH_SAFETY_MULTIPLIER=${OLLAMA_GRAPH_SAFETY_MULTIPLIER:-}
      - NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all
      - NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=compute,utility
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "/usr/bin/ollama", "list"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 5s

volumes:
  ollama-data:
    external: true

    ports:

      # auto-enable it on the experimental cc>=7.0 cards. Set OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1

      - OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=${OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE:-f16}

      # models (deepseek-r1:32b) on the K80's small dies instead of offloading to CPU.

      # risks "failed to allocate compute buffers". Unset = use the built-in 2.5 default.
      - OLLAMA_GRAPH_SAFETY_MULTIPLIER=${OLLAMA_GRAPH_SAFETY_MULTIPLIER:-}
      - NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all
      - NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=compute,utility
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "/usr/bin/ollama", "list"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 5s

# `docs/reports/` — K80 fleet characterization

Measured reports on how models behave on the 4 × Tesla K80, grouped by model family and swept over
context length. Two paired axes plus the kept #352 baseline.

## Versioning

Each sweep produces a **new immutable snapshot** named
`<report>-<YYYY-MM-DD>-<build-sha>.md` — so every report is tied to the exact ollama build it
measured. **Diff two snapshots of the same axis to see what changed between builds** (a throughput
or VRAM delta is then provably a code change, not measurement drift). Snapshots are never edited in
place or mixed across builds; the pre-versioning (mixed-build) reports live in git history.

> The `<build-sha>` is the ollama commit that was deployed and measured. Until the build embeds its
> own SHA (tracked follow-up — `/api/version` currently returns a static `2.1.0`), the SHA is
> recovered from the deploying pipeline run and recorded in each snapshot's `Build` row.

## Reports

### Speed/fit axis — VRAM / throughput

| Snapshot | Build | Swept | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`…-2026-07-10-d83061de.md`](./k80-vram-by-family-2026-07-10-d83061de.md) | `d83061de` | 2026-07-10 | **Latest.** 14 models (+`lfm2.5:8b`, new `lfm2` family, ~33 tok/s). No-harm vs `c282ba37`: 49/51 rows within ±3 %. gemma4:26b @8k+ now spreads to 4 dies (−9 %) — gemma4/KV-graph effect, not lfm2. |
| [`…-2026-06-29-c282ba37.md`](./k80-vram-by-family-2026-06-29-c282ba37.md) | `c282ba37` | 2026-06-29 | First clean single-build sweep (all 13 models). gemma4:12b now on GPU; `swa_full` windowed cache reclaims its 16k VRAM. e4b@2k cold-load artifact published + flagged. |

Here's what I have so far; two background sweeps (fork source patches, CI harness) are still running and I'll fold their findings in when they land.

## Ollama37 — a fork of Ollama that keeps the Tesla K80 alive

**The one-sentence version:** upstream Ollama dropped CUDA compute capability 3.7 (Kepler), so this fork pins the exact toolchain a 2014 K80 still needs and ships a ready-to-run Docker image that serves modern models — Gemma, Qwen, DeepSeek, gpt-oss — on $50 used datacenter hardware.

**The constraint chain that defines everything** (`README.md:66`): a K80 needs driver 470 → which pairs with CUDA 11.4 → which caps GCC at 10. Every design decision descends from that pin. It's also why the fork can't just take upstream code: `docs/porting-k80.md` states the discipline as *port the source, don't adapt the environment* — vendor upstream files in-tree and rewrite them to build with nvcc 11.4 / GCC 10 / sm_37, with cuBLAS or SIMT fallbacks where tensor cores would be used.

**Four moving parts:**

| Part | Where | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Build/toolchain | `CMakePresets.json:32`, `docker/builder/Dockerfile` | `CUDA 11 K80` preset compiles **native CUBIN** for `sm_37`–`sm_86`. `-real` not `-virtual` is deliberate: PTX would re-JIT 3–4 min on every container start |
| Two-image build | `docker/Makefile`, `docker/runtime/Dockerfile` | ~15 GB builder (CUDA 11.4, GCC 10 + CMake 4 from source, ~90 min first time) compiles; only artifacts land in a ~1 GB `rockylinux:8-minimal` runtime |
| Fork runtime patches | `llm/memory.go:402`, `ml/backend/ggml` | K80-calibrated behavior — e.g. the graph safety multiplier tuned to 2.5 because 3.5 over-reserved on 12 GB dies and pushed `deepseek-r1:32b` to CPU with VRAM free (#352) |
| CI / measurement | `cicd/`, `.github/workflows/`, `docs/reports/` | Self-hosted GPU runners, YAML testcases, and immutable per-build measurement snapshots |

**The most interesting cultural thing about this repo** is that it treats *measurement as the deliverable*, not an afterthought. `docs/porting-k80.md:20` makes the rule explicit: an upstream "optimization" tuned for tensor cores can be a net **loss** on sm_37 — flash attention turned out to be a 7.4× regression at 6,800 tokens, which a short-prompt benchmark would have hidden entirely. So FA ships *off* (`docker/docker-compose.yml:22`), and `docs/reports/README.md` versions every sweep as `<report>-<date>-<build-sha>.md` so a throughput delta between two snapshots is provably a code change rather than drift.

Two corollaries in the tooling: CI never triggers on `push`/`pull_request` (self-hosted runners on a public repo = arbitrary fork code execution), and `runs-on` must name a compute-capability label — `sm37`, `sm61`, `sm86` — because a K80 sweep that lands on a consumer card yields numbers that look valid and aren't.

There's also a second, more experimental track: an **MLX-CUDA port** to sm_37 under `x/mlx` (issue #188), shimming missing CUDA 11.4 libcu++/FP8 headers and porting kernels one at a time.

Your working tree has two untracked local files — `build.sh` (host-side build bypassing Docker) and `gpt-oss-20b-64k.Modelfile` (a 64k-context variant).

entries.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID ("name@team") or bare teammate name as task_id

- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

content.text:
Verified the key claims against source. Here's the full picture.

# Ollama37

**A fork of Ollama that keeps the Tesla K80 usable.** Upstream dropped CUDA compute capability 3.7 (Kepler), so this fork pins the exact toolchain a 2014 datacenter card still needs and ships a ready-to-run image serving modern models — Gemma, Qwen, DeepSeek, gpt-oss — on hardware you can buy used for very little.

## The constraint that explains every decision

```
K80 (sm_37) → driver 470 (last Kepler branch) → CUDA 11.4 → GCC 10 (CUDA 11.4's cap)
              no tensor cores · 12 GB per die
```

Every choice in the repo descends from that chain. It's also why the fork can't consume upstream code as-is. `docs/porting-k80.md` states the doctrine: **port the source, don't adapt the environment** — vendor upstream files in-tree and rewrite them to compile under nvcc 11.4 / GCC 10 / sm_37, with cuBLAS or SIMT fallbacks where tensor cores would be. "If using upstream unmodified were acceptable, upstream Ollama would already be the answer."

The fork is overwhelmingly **additive** — roughly 14.5k insertions against 200 deletions since the K80 restoration point (`ef14fb5b`, Nov 2025). It is not a patch-set fighting upstream logic.

## Five categories of change

**1. Build / toolchain — the literal "sm_37 restore."** `CMakePresets.json:32` adds a `CUDA 11 K80` preset: nine `-real` arches (`37,50,52,60,61,70,75,80,86`). All `-real`, never `-virtual` — PTX would re-JIT for 3–4 minutes on *every* container start. `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES` is set nowhere in `CMakeLists.txt`, so the preset name is the single arch knob. A nice tell of how far the pin reaches: `ggml/src/CMakeLists.txt:334` registers the `alderlake` CPU variant *without* AVX_VNNI, because `-mavxvnni` needs GCC 11+.

**2. Kernel patches for pre-Volta silicon.** The biggest hand-patch is in `ggml-cuda.cu:2168-2261` — a two-tier fallback where `gemm_algo` drops from `CUBLAS_GEMM_DEFAULT_TENSOR_OP` to `CUBLAS_GEMM_DEFAULT` below Volta, and FP32 abandons the `*Ex` calls entirely for `cublasSgemmStridedBatched`, because the `Ex` variants return `CUBLAS_STATUS_ARCH_MISMATCH` on Kepler *regardless* of algo. `mma.cuh` substitutes a `__shfl_sync` software transpose where CUDA 11.4 lacks `movmatrix.sync.aligned` PTX. New non-tensor-core kernels (`cumsum.cu`, `solve-tri.cu`, `tri.cu`, `diag.cu`, `fill.cu`) back the DeltaNet ops.

**3. Memory policy for 12 GB dies.** Fork-specific tuning, all with measured justification in the comments:
- `llm/memory.go:402` — graph safety multiplier **2.5**, not upstream's 3.5, because 3.5 over-reserved per die and pushed `deepseek-r1:32b` to CPU with VRAM free (0.43 → 2.77 tok/s, #352).
- `llm/server.go:248` — per-architecture context-tiered `num_batch` clamp. With FA off, the Q·Kᵀ score buffer grows with batch, spreading a model across more PCIe-linked dies; the clamp picks the fewest-die batch that stays 100% on GPU.
- `ggml.go:184` — skips the MTP blocks qwen35 GGUFs count but never run, reclaiming 251–525 MiB (#489).
- `server/metrics.go` — a fork-added `/api/metrics` with per-GPU attribution and explicitly labeled "unaccounted" VRAM.

**4. Model architectures** (the largest line count, only indirectly K80-related): `model/models/qwen35/` with a 550-line `deltanet.go` — the README claims first Ollama fork to support the DeltaNet recurrent arch — plus `gemma4/` (text/vision/audio), qwen3.8 split-projector vision, and new renderers/parsers. Mirrored into vendored llama.cpp.

**5. An experimental MLX-CUDA track** under `x/mlx` (#188): shimming CUDA 11.4's missing libcu++/FP8 headers and porting MLX kernels to sm_37 one at a time.

## The thing that makes this repo distinctive

**It treats measurement as the deliverable.** `docs/porting-k80.md:20` makes it a rule: an upstream "optimization" tuned for tensor cores can be a net *loss* on sm_37. Flash attention was the worked example — a ~22% loss at short context but a **7.4× loss** at a 6,800-token prompt (1.18 vs 8.74 tok/s decode). A short-prompt benchmark would have hidden it entirely.

So FA ships off, and it's enforced in two paired places: `ml/device.go:436` restricts CUDA FA to *exactly* cc 7.0 (upstream allows cc ≥ 7), and `fattn-mma-f16.cuh:12` refuses the MMA_F16 kernel under CUDA 11.4 because the software `movmatrix` fallback returns NaN. That double gate is precisely why one image can safely carry CUBIN for sm_37 through sm_86.

`docs/reports/` versions every sweep as `<report>-<date>-<build-sha>.md`, never edited in place — so a throughput delta between two snapshots is *provably* a code change rather than measurement drift.

## The pipeline, end to end

```
docs/stories/STORY-NNN.md          the need
  → docs/tests/TS-NN-<suite>.md    scenario prose, bound by story_hash (green/stale/unbound)
  → cicd/tests/testcases/<suite>/TC-*.yml   executable: bash steps + expect/rejectPatterns
  → cicd/tests/src/cli.ts          the one runner (run, bench-*, test-mcp, judge)
  → simple judge always; agent judge on JUDGE_MODE=dual
  → cicd/results/ → docs/reports/ and docs/traces/ when worth remembering
```

26 testcases across four suites (build, runtime, inference, models). The **simple judge** is deterministic and model-free: exit codes, patterns, and a CUDA-error regex that treats `library=cpu` as a failure — it reads only step output, never container logs, because ollama's memory backoff emits *expected* `cudaMalloc` failures. The **agent judge** is an opt-in ACP client, one fresh session per test, all tool permissions refused, with a loop guard that cancels a turn on repeated phrases (real loops hit 385+; healthy reasoning peaked at 21). A test the simple judge already failed never reaches it.

Testcases do their real assertion work in bash and emit sentinels — `LOAD_OK`, `REPLY_REPEAT`, `GPU_COUNT_OK` — partly to keep a broken-but-nonempty reply away from the agent judge, which loops when asked to quote repeated text back. That's the same instinct as your standing preference: work model-output quirks around in the script, not in the library.

## Two operational rules worth internalizing

- **Never `runs-on: self-hosted` bare.** Select by compute capability — `sm37` (the K80 reference box), `sm61` (1080 Ti), `sm86` (3060). A K80 sweep that lands on a consumer card produces numbers that look valid and aren't. Host B's cards also serve the judge's ollama, so they run only `test-models.yml`.
- **Nothing triggers on `push`/`pull_request`** — self-hosted runners on a public repo would let a fork execute arbitrary code. Adding such a trigger is a security decision, not a convenience.

And the build/apply chain is deliberately encoded as skills rather than left to improvisation: build via CI (a local `make` defaults `OLLAMA_VERSION=0.0.0` and the registry then rejects gated pulls with 412), and `TC-BUILD-004`'s `docker tag ollama37:latest dogkeeper886/ollama37:latest` is the hinge that makes a fresh build the image compose actually reads. Running a single `test_id` skips that retag — every later test then silently exercises stale code.

---

Your tree has two untracked local files: `build.sh` (bare-metal build, same preset, bypassing Docker) and `gpt-oss-20b-64k.Modelfile` (a 64k-context variant).

Want me to turn this into a shareable onboarding page, or go deeper on any one layer?

########## PR #515 ##########
TITLE: fix(#513): read the server under test from the host, and let a shared host lend a GPU
MERGED: 2026-09-27T05:00:39Z

The models suite keeps each test's server log for the report and the agent judge, and every suite reaches the server by container name and address. The testbeds now include a second host that starts its ollama37 container from a systemd unit, pinned to one card, and whose GPUs also serve the agent judge. Its runs lost the server log, because the collector only read `docker compose logs`, and every hard-coded `ollama37` and `localhost:11434` pointed at the wrong server. The pipeline now reads its server under test from each runner's `.env`, follows the container's log by name, and on a shared host lends a card to the test and returns it before judging.

Refs #513. This PR does not close it: the compose-started run on the K80 host is still to verify.

## Details

- **Host knobs:** `cicd/tests/src/config.ts` sets `OLLAMA37_CONTAINER` (`ollama37`) and `OLLAMA_HOST` (`http://localhost:11434`) unless the environment does. A runner's `.env` overrides them per host, so host A needs no change.
- **Log collector:** follows `docker logs --follow $OLLAMA37_CONTAINER`, stdout and stderr merged into one ordered stream, however the container was started.
- **Testcases:** every suite uses `$OLLAMA37_CONTAINER` (48 places) and `$OLLAMA_HOST` (90). TC-RUNTIME-001 drops its container-name pattern; `compose ps` already scopes to the project.
- **Workflows:** the job-level `OLLAMA_HOST` is removed so the runner's `.env` wins; shell steps fall back with `${VAR:-default}`. `test-mlx-smoke.yml` stops and starts the production container by `OLLAMA37_CONTAINER`.
- **Subset:** `OLLAMA37_TEST_IDS` limits `cli.ts run` to a host's testcases.
- **Tests before judge:** `cli.ts run` saves `results.json`, and the new `cli.ts judge <dir>` judges it in a later step.
- **Shared host (`test-models.yml`):** Yield GPU stops `OLLAMA37_YIELD_SERVICE` and starts `OLLAMA37_SERVICE` (user systemd units). Restore GPU (`always()`) gives the card back if the yielded service is enabled, and the agent judge then runs on the saved results. Hosts that set neither key skip both steps.
- **Docs:** `cicd/docs/` is removed; the rewritten `cicd/README.md` maps folder → command → host knobs, with SVG sources in `docs/diagrams/` and `docs/diagrams/render.sh`.
- **Verified:** on host B (RTX 3060), TC-MODELS-003 passed both judges through yield → run → unload → restore → judge, run by hand with the runner's `.env`. Type check clean; all YAML parses; README commands, paths, env vars and links checked against the code.
- **Not verified:** a compose-started run on host A (offline), and a CI run on host B (its runner is not registered yet).
- **Known gap:** on the GTX 1080 Ti the die check fails `GPU_COUNT_EXCEEDED`, because a second 99 MiB compute process sits on that card. The 3060 passes.

########## PR #518 ##########
TITLE: fix(#516): offer the runners that exist — sm37, sm61, sm86 — and drop sm75
MERGED: 2026-09-27T05:57:57Z

Every workflow is dispatched to a GPU testbed by its `runner_label` input. Host B now runs two runners, `sm61` (GTX 1080 Ti) and `sm86` (RTX 3060), and the RTX 2060 behind `sm75` is gone. Each workflow's `choice` input still listed only `sm37` and `sm75`, so GitHub refused the new labels with HTTP 422 and still offered a runner that no longer exists. The options now list the three runners that exist, and the rules and skills an agent reads to pick a label match them.

Refs #516. This meets its first Done When item. It does not meet the second: a GitHub variable can't fill `options:` (`on.workflow_dispatch.inputs` evaluates no contexts), so a runner change still means editing the workflow files.

## Details

- **Workflows (11):** `runner_label` options `[sm37, sm61, sm86]`, default `sm37`. Each description names the GTX 1080 Ti and RTX 3060 and keeps its own caveat, e.g. `test-models.yml` says the runner's `OLLAMA37_TEST_IDS` picks the models that fit.
- **Agent rules:** `.claude/rules/workflow-patterns.md` host table gets `sm61` / `sm86` rows (one card each, models suite only), and the K80 runner is renamed `rocky8-k80-cicd-1`, as GitHub lists it.
- **Skills:** `ollama37-ci-apply`, `-build` and `-perf` rewritten as description + steps (skill-structure). They use `sm37`, and say host B is models-only. The fit-map sweep section leaves `ollama37-ci-perf`; `workflow-patterns.md` still covers that workflow.
- **Testcase:** TC-RUNTIME-002's notes list the current labels.
- **Differs from the plan on #516:** the skills don't offer `sm61` / `sm86` for apply, build or perf, and the perf example uses `sm37`, not `sm86`. Those workflows `docker compose up` on every GPU and port 11434, which would clash with host B's judge `ollama`; only `test-models.yml` lends a card and gives it back.
- **Known gap:** the dropdowns still offer `sm61` / `sm86` on those compose workflows; a dispatch there would fail.
- **Verify after merge:** `gh workflow run test-models.yml -f runner_label=sm86 -f test_id=TC-MODELS-016` creates a run instead of the 422.

########## PR #521 ##########
TITLE: fix(#519): count the GPUs the container's own processes use, not every process
MERGED: 2026-09-27T06:39:24Z

The models suite checks that a model spreads over no more GPUs than its footprint needs, because a model that spills onto an extra K80 die loses speed on the cross-die traffic. On host B's GTX 1080 Ti, a desktop app holds its own CUDA context: `zed-editor`, 111 MiB. The check counted every process `nvidia-smi` lists, and inside the container that includes host processes, so gemma4:e2b sitting wholly on one card read as `Active GPUs: 2` and failed `GPU_COUNT_EXCEEDED`. The check now counts only the distinct GPUs used by the container's own processes.

Refs #519. This meets its first Done When item. The second, that a real multi-die spill still fails on `sm37`, waits for host A.

## Details

- **Change:** `die_check` in the 18 model testcases keeps the `nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps` rows whose pid belongs to `$OLLAMA37_CONTAINER` (`docker top`), and counts their distinct `gpu_uuid`. The total, the 11441 MiB die rule, the one reload and the `GPU_COUNT_OK` / `GPU_COUNT_EXCEEDED` strings are unchanged.
- **Why pid, not name:** inside the container `nvidia-smi` reports every `process_name` as `[Not Found]`, ollama's own included.
- **Why a real spill still fails:** a model spread over K80 dies lists its runner pid once per die, each with a different `gpu_uuid`.
- **Verified on sm61:** run [36300391663](https://github.com/dogkeeper886/ollama37/actions/runs/36300391663) from this branch — `zed-editor` on the card, model 36/36 layers on GPU, `Active GPUs: 1`, `GPU_COUNT_OK`, both judges PASS. The same test failed on `main` in run [36299330869](https://github.com/dogkeeper886/ollama37/actions/runs/36299330869).
- **Not verified:** a multi-die spill on `sm37`, and that the K80's driver 470 accepts `gpu_uuid` in `--query-compute-apps` (host A is offline).
- **Left as is:** the presence checks ("Check GPU memory" in the models suite, TC-INFERENCE-002) only expect some `MiB` in the list, so another process's context also satisfies them.

content.content:
########## #513 ##########
- Workflows drop the job-level `OLLAMA_HOST`, so the runner's `.env` wins.
- `docker-compose.yml` reads `container_name` from `OLLAMA37_CONTAINER`.

### 2. Host B switches its GPUs per job

Host B's main use is `ollama` on both cards, which is also the agent judge (`JUDGE_BASE_URL`). A model-test job borrows one card and gives it back:

```
Yield GPU     (only if OLLAMA37_SERVICE is set)
  stop any ollama37-* unit left running
  ollama active? → stop it
  start $OLLAMA37_SERVICE → wait for /api/tags
Run models tests       JUDGE_MODE=simple (execute only)
Restore GPU   if: always()
  stop $OLLAMA37_SERVICE
  ollama enabled? → start it → wait for /api/tags
Agent judge            cli.ts judge <results>, now that the judge is back
```

- Runners and ollama37 units are separate; there are no `BindsTo`/`Wants`. One runner per card, as user services, so a job can run `systemctl --user`.
- The Restore step starts `ollama` if it's *enabled*, not "if it was running". A job killed mid-run then heals on the next job.
- Tests before judge needs a new `cli.ts judge` subcommand. Today `cli.ts run` executes and judges in one process, while the judge's server is down.

### 3. Host A is unchanged

No new `.env` keys. The Yield and Restore steps skip, and the defaults match today's values. The only difference is that execute and judge become two steps.

### Constraints accepted

- **One job at a time on host B.** The 1080 Ti and 3060 runners would clash on port 11434; there's a single user, so this is by convention.
- **Host A's agent judge needs host B idle with `ollama` up.** Don't overlap a host A dual-judge run with a host B test window. If that ever matters, the judge client waits for `JUDGE_BASE_URL`.

### Open

- **The die check counts every compute process on the visible GPU.** On the GTX 1080 Ti, TC-MODELS-003 loaded fully (29/29 layers, logs captured through the new collector) but failed `GPU_COUNT_EXCEEDED`: a second 99 MiB process sat on the card. The check also hard-codes the K80 die size, 11441 MiB.
- **Runner registration for host B is still to do.**

content.text:
Read all six. Here's the picture, with the host-A angle up front.

## Verdict

Six PRs merged today, every one CI — three fixes and three session-log catch-ups. All three issues (#513, #516, #519) were closed, each with a comment naming what was *not* verified first. **Two of those unverified items were waiting specifically on host A, which is where we're sitting now** — and I could already settle one of them from the shell.

## The three fixes

| PR | Issue | What changed | Left open |
|---|---|---|---|
| #515 | #513 | Log collector follows `docker logs --follow $OLLAMA37_CONTAINER` instead of `docker compose logs`; every testcase reads `$OLLAMA37_CONTAINER` (48 places) and `$OLLAMA_HOST` (90); `cli.ts run` and `cli.ts judge` split so a shared host can lend a GPU and get it back before judging | **A compose-started run on host A** (Done When #3) — host A was offline |
| #518 | #516 | `runner_label` options `[sm37, sm61, sm86]`, `sm75` dropped; rules + the three `ollama37-ci-*` skills updated to match | Done When #2 dropped by decision — `on.workflow_dispatch.inputs` evaluates no contexts, so a GitHub variable can't fill `options:`. Gap: the dropdowns still offer `sm61`/`sm86` on compose workflows where a dispatch would clash with host B's judge |
| #521 | #519 | `die_check` now keeps only the `nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps` rows whose pid belongs to the container (`docker top`), then counts distinct `gpu_uuid` — a desktop `zed-editor` context no longer reads as a second active GPU | **A real multi-die spill still failing on sm37** (Done When #2), and whether driver 470 accepts `gpu_uuid` |

## What host A owes, and one item already closed

I confirmed this box: 4 × Tesla K80, 11441 MiB each, driver **470.256.02** — matching the 11441 die constant in `die_check`.

**`gpu_uuid` works on 470.** `nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,gpu_uuid,used_memory` returns its header cleanly, while `--query-gpu=compute_cap` on the same driver errors with `Field "compute_cap" is not a valid field to query`. So the field genuinely is supported, not silently ignored — that half of #521's gap is answered.

The mechanism is sound for a reason neither PR spells out: the NVIDIA driver reports **host** PIDs even when `nvidia-smi` runs inside the container, which is exactly what `docker top` lists — and also why every `process_name` comes back `[Not Found]`, since those pids aren't in the container's own `/proc`. Matching on pid rather than name is the right call.

**What still can't be answered yet:** the container is `Exited (128) 4 days ago`, so nothing is loaded. Both remaining verifications need it recreated first — and host A is the only testbed that *can* prove the spill case, since #521's evidence came from single-card hosts where a spill is impossible by construction.

One latent gap I noticed in the code as it stands: with no container processes on GPU, `active` is 0, so `[ "$active" -le 1 ]` short-circuits true and `die_check` passes vacuously on a CPU-only load. The separate "Check GPU memory" presence step is what actually catches that, and PR #521 already flags those presence checks as loose.

## The session log thread

All three log PRs extend **one file** — `.sessions/cf5a3839-…jsonl`, the host-B session — re-scrubbed each time against the local denylist outside the repo (`~/.claude/scrub-denylist.txt`): 47 → 60 → 65 lines redacted, `scan` clean, valid JSON throughout. #517 also deleted `.sessions/README.md`, since `ls` lists the logs and the scrub steps live in the script's docstring.

The pattern worth naming: **each new issue links the log, but the committed snapshot always stops before the work that followed it**, so a fresh PR is needed just to catch it up. That happened three times in one day for the same file. And it's stale again right now — #520 says so explicitly: the `zed-editor` pid identification and the container-pid fix that became #521 aren't in the committed copy.

The one structural fix would be capturing the log at issue *close* rather than at filing, or scrubbing on a hook. Worth raising as its own issue if the churn keeps up.

---

Working tree is clean against `origin/main` apart from your two untracked files.

The natural next step here is the apply-then-verify chain the skills encode: confirm a retag, recreate the container via `test-runtime.yml` on `sm37` (which settles #513's Done When #3 as a side effect), then run a models test with a model large enough to spread across dies to prove `GPU_COUNT_EXCEEDED` still fires. Want me to start that, or dig further into any of these PRs first?

# CI-only override: serve models from the CI host's model store.
#
# The only difference from docker-compose.yml is where models come from. The
# testbed's store is an NFS share mounted on the host, bind-mounted here over
# /root/.ollama/models; everything else (image, port, keys in the ollama-data
# volume) is the public compose file, so CI keeps exercising what users run.
#
# The CI host enables it through the runner's .env, not the workflows:
#   COMPOSE_FILE=docker-compose.yml:docker-compose.ci.yml
#   OLLAMA37_MODELS_DIR=/path/to/models
# Every `docker compose` call runs from docker/, so the relative paths resolve.
#
# Models are pulled from the host as the share's owner; the container only
# reads them, so NFS root squashing never applies.
services:
  ollama:
    volumes:
      - ${OLLAMA37_MODELS_DIR:?OLLAMA37_MODELS_DIR must be set on the CI host}:/root/.ollama/models

Full preflight done on host A. Here's the checklist, bottom-up as you asked.

## Preflight — host A (`rocky8-k80-cicd-1`, 4 × Tesla K80)

| # | Layer | State | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **`ollama37` service file** — `~/.config/systemd/user/ollama.service` | `ExecStart=/home/jack/src/ollama37/dist/bin/ollama serve` (your bare-metal `build.sh` binary), **active, enabled**, `Restart=always`, pid 2655 holding `127.0.0.1:11434`. Drop-in `require-nfs.conf` gates on the models mountpoint | ✋ **BLOCKER** |
| 2 | **Runner service file** — `actions.runner.dogkeeper886-ollama37.rocky8-k80-cicd-1.service` | System unit, `User=jack`, `WorkingDirectory=/home/jack/actions-runner`, active. GitHub: **online, idle**, labels `[self-hosted, Linux, X64, sm37]` | ✓ |
| 3 | **Runner `.env`** — `/home/jack/actions-runner/.env` | `COMPOSE_FILE=docker-compose.yml:docker-compose.ci.yml`, `OLLAMA37_MODELS_DIR=/home/jack/.ollama/models`. No `OLLAMA37_CONTAINER`/`OLLAMA_HOST` → defaults `ollama37` / `localhost:11434`. No `OLLAMA37_SERVICE` → yield/restore skip, exactly as #515 intended for host A | ✓ |
| 4 | **Compose pair** — `docker/docker-compose.yml` + `.ci.yml` | CI override bind-mounts the NFS store over `/root/.ollama/models`; enabled via the runner `.env` above, not the workflows | ✓ |
| 5 | **Model store** | NFS `PRIVATE-IP:/home/jack/ollama-models`, mounted, 328 G used / 906 G, 15 families incl. `gpt-oss-64k`. The `ollama-data` volume holds only SSH keys (8 K) — correct, models arrive via the bind | ✓ |
| 6 | **Image + tags** | `ollama37:latest` = `82feb218ba9d`, built 2026-09-22 07:21, also tagged `dogkeeper886/ollama37:v2.3.1`. **`dogkeeper886/ollama37:latest` is absent locally** — compose pins it, so it would pull from Hub instead of using your build | ✋ **retag needed** |
| 7 | **Image currency** | Newest image-source commit on `main` is `2ea906a2` (#509 ghost contexts, Sep 21 22:54) — **predates the Sep 22 07:21 build**. Today's six PRs touched zero image code. **No rebuild required** | ✓ |
| 8 | **GPU baseline** | 4 × K80, 11441 MiB each, driver 470.256.02, **all dies 0 MiB, no compute apps** — a clean baseline for the die check | ✓ |
| 9 | **UVM devices** | `/dev/nvidia-uvm` + `-uvm-tools` present — the classic "0 GPUs" snag isn't in play | ✓ |
| 10 | **Temp guard** | User unit inactive/disabled, but irrelevant: workflows wrap the run in `cicd/scripts/gpu-temp-guard.sh`, exit 75 = overheat → job fails | ✓ |
| 11 | **CI env `cicd-1`** | `OLLAMA_VERSION=2.3.1` (matches the `v2.3.1` tag), `JUDGE_BASE_URL=http://PRIVATE-IP:11434` (host B), `JUDGE_MODEL=gpt-oss-64k:20b`. All three runners idle, so a dual-judge run won't contend | ✓ |
| 12 | **gh auth / git** | `dogkeeper886` with `workflow` scope; `main` clean against `origin/main` | ✓ |

## The one real blocker, and why it's not just a port

The container's last death is recorded verbatim: `exit=128`, `listen tcp4 0.0.0.0:11434: bind: address already in use`, finished 2026-09-22T11:34Z. Your native `ollama.service` took 11434 and the container has been down since.

The subtler hazard is that **leaving it up is worse than a clean failure**. With the native server on 11434 and no container, `cli.ts` would happily drive inference against the bare-metal binary while every `docker exec` / `docker top` step errors — precisely the wrong-server class of bug #515 existed to kill.

And host A has no automatic escape: the Yield step gates on `OLLAMA37_SERVICE` (`test-models.yml:83` — `[ -n "${OLLAMA37_SERVICE:-}" ] || exit 0`), so setting `OLLAMA37_YIELD_SERVICE` alone does nothing, and `test-runtime.yml` has no yield step at all. Today it's a manual stop. That gap looks worth its own issue — host A can't yield its native server the way host B yields its judge.

## Chain I'll run once that's settled

1. Stop `ollama.service` → 11434 free
2. `gh workflow run test-build.yml --ref main -f runner_label=sm37 -f test_id=TC-BUILD-004` → retag, expect `retagged sha256:`
3. `gh workflow run test-runtime.yml --ref main -f runner_label=sm37` → compose down/up with the CI override + health poll. **This is #513's Done When #3** — the compose-started run on host A that was never done
4. `gh run watch <id> --exit-status`
5. Then `test-inference.yml`, then `test-models.yml` — and for #519's Done When #2 I'd force a genuine bad spill (e.g. `OLLAMA_SCHED_SPREAD=1` on a model whose total fits one die) so `GPU_COUNT_EXCEEDED` has to fire. I'll confirm that model choice with you before running it.

Step 1 is your call — it kills your interactive server, and it's `enabled`, so it returns on reboot either way.

## Chain status — and #513 is *not* actually met

**Progress**
1. ✅ `ollama.service` stopped, 11434 free
2. ✅ Retagged `dogkeeper886/ollama37:latest` → `82feb218ba9d` (v2.3.1)
3. ✅ `test-runtime.yml` on sm37 — [36307261342](https://github.com/dogkeeper886/ollama37/actions/runs/36307261342), **4/4 passed**. Container `Up (healthy)` on the right image, NFS bind attached, 328 GB of models visible inside
4. 🔄 Runtime re-run [36307521518](https://github.com/dogkeeper886/ollama37/actions/runs/36307521518) as a differential test

**But the green tick is hiding the very failure #513 was filed about.** Buried in the passing run:

```
[WARN] Failed to start log collector: Error: Log collector failed to start
```

I traced it end to end, and the evidence is on this host:

`/tmp/ollama37-session-1790498799824.log` was created at `08:46:39.825Z` — today's run — and holds **13,632 lines dated 2026-09-21T15:20 → 2026-09-22T11:34**. It captured the *dead container's five-day-old backlog* and nothing from today.

The mechanism:

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| `log-collector.ts:363` | spawns `docker logs --follow --timestamps ollama37` — but the container was `Exited (128)`, so Docker dumps the backlog and **exits immediately** |
| `log-collector.ts:88-99` | the `close` handler clears `isRunning` before the 500 ms probe → `reject('Log collector failed to start')` |
| `executor.ts:288` | catches it and sets `this.logCollector = null` — **disabling capture for the entire run** |
| TC-RUNTIME-001's `reconnectLogs: true` | can never fire; there's no collector object left to reconnect |
| the judge | never sees a server log, and nothing fails, because it's a `WARN` |

So the trigger is **a cold start** — the container not running when the suite begins. That's structural for the runtime suite, whose first test is `compose down` + `up -d`. Host B never hit it because its systemd-started container was already up when the models suite ran. That's why #513 looked fixed there.

This is a different bug from the one #515 fixed (compose-only vs. `docker logs`), so it wants its own issue rather than reopening #513 — and it's the second masked-failure pattern today, after the die check counting host processes. Both were invisible while CI stayed green.

The re-run will settle the diagnosis: with the container up at start, I expect `[LOG] Docker log collector started` and live logs in a fresh session file. If that's what we see, the fix is small — have `start()` tolerate a not-running container and let `reconnect()` attach once it's up, instead of nulling the collector for the whole run.

I'll hold the inference and models steps until this comes back, then carry on to the `GPU_COUNT_EXCEEDED` proof. For that one I've confirmed the forcing function exists: `OLLAMA_SCHED_SPREAD` is live in this fork (`envconfig/config.go:198`, and the server log shows `OLLAMA_SCHED_SPREAD:false`), so spreading a small model like `gemma3:270m` across all four dies would make `total` fit in `active-1` dies and force the check to fire. That needs a container recreate with the extra env, so I'll check with you before doing it.

## The differential is decisive

| | Run 1 — container **down** at start | Run 2 — container **up** at start |
|---|---|---|
| Collector | `[WARN] Failed to start log collector` | `[LOG] Docker log collector started on ollama37` → `[LOG] Reconnected log collector` → `stopped` |
| Session file | 13,632 lines, **all Sep 21–22** | 192 lines, **all 192 dated 2026-09-27** |
| Test markers | **0** | **8** (4 tests × start/end) |
| Result | 4/4 passed | 4/4 passed |

Same workflow, same commit, same host, four minutes apart. The only variable was whether the container was running when the suite began.

**So #513's Done When #3 is genuinely met** — on a warm start, a compose-started container on host A has its log followed by name, with per-test markers intact. That's the thing host B could never demonstrate.

**And the cold-start path is a separate, silent bug.** `start()` treats "container not running" as fatal, `executor.ts:288` nulls the collector for the whole run, and `reconnectLogs` — which demonstrably works, as Run 2 shows — never gets the chance. The fix is narrow: let `start()` tolerate a stopped container and leave the collector armed for `reconnect()` to attach, instead of discarding it. Worth an issue with this differential as the evidence, since it's reproducible on demand.

🔄 Inference suite running: [36307618035](https://github.com/dogkeeper886/ollama37/actions/runs/36307618035)

## One decision coming on the models step

The full models suite is 19 testcases across models up to `qwen3.6:35b` — a multi-hour K80 sweep, and mostly re-treading what host B already covered today. For #519's remaining item I'd rather run two targeted cases:

- **Positive:** `TC-MODELS-002` (`gemma3:27b`) — genuinely spans 2+ dies, so it proves the pid filter *retains* per-die rows on driver 470 rather than collapsing a legitimate multi-die model to `Active GPUs: 1`. This is the half that matters most, because a false `1` would silently disable the check forever.
- **Negative:** force a real over-spread with `OLLAMA_SCHED_SPREAD=1` on a small model (`gemma3:270m`), so `total` fits in `active-1` dies and `GPU_COUNT_EXCEEDED` *has* to fire.

The negative test needs the container recreated with that env, which puts it outside a stock CI dispatch — I'd do it as a deliberate, logged experiment and revert to the baseline afterward, the way `test-context.yml` handles its flash-attention env. Say the word on whether you want the negative test at all, or just the positive one plus the full suite.
